Now Britain must export its goods to Europe under WTO rules, and therefore faces greater tariffs.

It's true that British companies are no longer forced to deal with seemingly arbitrary rules imposed by other EU countries, and can set their own. So that's likely appealing to British-based smaller businesses, but it also adds a layer of complexity when having to deal with the regulations of other countries. Harmonizing regulations across Europe made that much simpler.

Being alone also puts them in a weaker negotiation position. The EU is a massive economic trade bloc, so other countries see it as an appealing partner for trade deals. Now now that Britain is by itself, it is a smaller economic entity, and would therefore be valued less in terms of trade negotiations.

It seems to me the support to leave is influenced too much by misguided ideas that it would reduce immigration. It won't. The EU didn't force Europe to accept people in, and it didn't hinder their ability to police the shores to prevent illegal border jumpers.
The more important question: Who benefits from leaving? I'm not talking average joes, I'm talking people with influence.

The biggest one is stability. Businesses hate instability. It makes it hard to invest in new things (technologies, people, expansions) when the future is uncertain. Higher risk/reward. I'm no fan of big business but to think that tearing up the trade agreements is going to get them to write new ones that benefit the little guy is downright naive.

Another issue (more so for younger folks) is the mobility provided by the EU. Similar to state lines in US, you could pretty much get a job in an EU country, move there, buy a house, have kids, move to another country, work there, and retire in another one. Little paperwork was involved. Now the process will go thru visas, which will not only decrease the mobility but provide incentives for businesses to hire domestically. Good if UK is the job capital of EU, not so good if it's not.

There's a good many reasons.

  • The UK, let alone what may in the near future become England alone, will never regain the sort of economic or military dominance it once had. Staying as a part of a larger whole would give it more of a voice in international matters. As just one example even the presidency of the EU rotates between nations. During the UK's time, it would be the leader of one of the most powerful nation groups in the world. That opportunity is now gone.

  • Freedom of travel, work, and education. For those within the EU they're free to live, work, go to school, and basically do as they see fit in whatever country they like. That's an enormous amount of freedom and flexibility which will now be gone and replaced with paperwork, visas, limited residency permits and so on.

  • Empathy. I think there's something a bit peculiar about this world. I, through no merit of my own, was popped into existence about 50 miles north of an imaginary line. A line created by people dead for hundreds of years. Since I was born north of this line I was guaranteed at least very good chance of a reasonable existence even if I ended up a not so productive or good person. If instead I had happened to have been born to the south of this imaginary line I'd have been equally guaranteed a extremely high chance of living a pretty shitty existence even if I was an extremely productive and good person. Am I willing to live a moderately less pleasant life in hopes of in the future having those born to the south of this line having a more reasonable chance at a better life as well? For those with any degree of empathy, this is not a pleasant question to face since either answer hurts.

  • Business opportunity. The more areas you can legally operate within the more potential to find your own little niche in the market and world in general. Of course this also comes with increased competition so there's some balance there but it comes down to would you rather be a small fish in a small pool with not many other fish or a small fish in a big pool with lots of other fish.

  • Benefits in legislation. The EU has generally been very pro consumer. Many of the consumer rights and protections citizens of EU nations enjoy are precisely because of the EU. For instance one that really stood out to me was the EU enforcing first-sale doctrine. This provides some information on the case, but essentially the EU affirmed that licensing or purchasing something is in reality no different. Once something is 'licensed' to you, you own it and are free to do with it as you please - including selling it to somebody else even if the company in question tries to argue that you can't because their terms and conditions say you can't. Huge win for the consumer. One could argue that this is an effect of the size of the EU. Corrupting smaller bodies of law is far easier than corrupting larger ones - particularly when those larger ones are in no way homogenous.

I don't have a stance on remain vs leave. I consider myself inadequately informed to make a decision, though I do think I'm well enough informed enough to formulate cohesive arguments for both sides.
